blocks.text: A permutation is an ordered arrangement of items, where the same set arranged in a different order counts as a genuinely different result. Counting how many such arrangements exist is one of the most fundamental and widely used tools in combinatorics.

blocks.caption: The core ideas this lesson connects together

blocks.text: 1. What a Permutation Is
A permutation is an arrangement of items where order matters, the sequence A, B, C is considered a different permutation from C, B, A even though both use the exact same 3 letters.

code.content:
from itertools import permutations
result = list(permutations(["A", "B", "C"]))
print(result)   # 6 different orderings of the same 3 letters

blocks.text: This order-sensitivity is the single defining feature that separates a permutation from a combination, covered in the very next lesson, where order is deliberately ignored instead.
The word permutation comes from a Latin root meaning to change thoroughly, fitting given how completely rearranging a sequence changes its identity as a distinct ordering.

A quick way to check understanding, listing out all permutations of a very small set by hand and confirming the count matches the factorial formula, is a good habit before relying on the formula for larger sets.
2. Arranging All n Items: n Factorial
The number of ways to arrange all n distinct items in a sequence is n factorial, written n!, computed as n times n minus 1 times n minus 2, continuing down to 1.

code.content:
import math
print(math.factorial(3))   # 6, matching the 6 permutations of A, B, C
print(math.factorial(5))   # 120

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: 4 factorial equals 4 times 3 times 2 times 1, which is 24, matching exactly the 24 distinct orderings of 4 distinct letters.

blocks.text: Factorial values grow extremely quickly, 10 factorial already exceeds 3.6 million, and 20 factorial exceeds the number of atoms in a small physical object, illustrating just how fast this counting grows.
3. Why n Factorial Counts All Arrangements

This formula follows directly from the fundamental counting principle covered in the combinatorics lesson, there are n choices for the first position, n minus 1 remaining choices for the second position, and so on, multiplying all these choices together gives n factorial.
Recognizing this connection means the n factorial formula never needs to be memorized blindly, it can always be rederived directly from the fundamental counting principle whenever needed.
This same multiplicative reasoning extends naturally to the n permute r formula in the next section, simply stopping the multiplication after r terms instead of continuing all the way down to 1.
4. Permutations of a Subset: n Permute r

Often only r items out of a larger set of n need to be arranged, not all of them. The formula for this is n permute r = n factorial divided by (n minus r) factorial, counting only the ordered arrangements of the chosen r items.

Notice that n permute n, arranging all n items with no subset restriction, correctly reduces to plain n factorial, since dividing by (n minus n) factorial, which is 0 factorial, defined as 1, leaves the formula unchanged.
This formula is sometimes written using the notation P(n, r) instead of the words n permute r, both refer to the identical calculation.
5. A Worked Example: Ranking Top 3 Finishers
If 8 runners compete in a race, how many different possible orderings are there for who finishes 1st, 2nd, and 3rd?

code.content: print(n_permute_r(8, 3))   # 336 possible orderings of the top 3 finishers

blocks.text: This same style of calculation applies directly to any leaderboard or ranking scenario, awards ceremonies, competition standings, or search result rankings all count orderings in exactly this way.
Notice this counts only the top 3 positions specifically, the remaining 5 runners finishing positions do not factor into this particular calculation at all.
6. Permutations with Repetition Allowed

When repetition is allowed, such as choosing a 4-digit PIN where digits can repeat, the count is simply n raised to the power r, rather than the standard permutation formula, since each position independently has n choices regardless of what was chosen before.

code.content: print(10 ** 4)   # 10000 possible 4-digit PINs, with repetition allowed

blocks.text: This repetition-allowed formula grows even faster than the standard permutation formula for the same n and r, since no items are ever removed from the pool of available choices.
This same formula applies directly to counting possible license plates, passwords with repeated characters allowed, or any other fixed-length code where each position is chosen independently.
The 10000 possible PINs computed here also directly explains why a 4-digit PIN alone provides fairly weak security compared to a longer password using a larger character set.
7. Permutations of a Set with Duplicate Items

When some items in the set to be arranged are identical, the plain n factorial count overcounts, since swapping two identical items produces an arrangement that looks the same. Dividing by the factorial of each repeated group size corrects for this overcounting.
Failing to divide out the duplicate group factorials is one of the most common counting errors, silently multiplying the true answer by an incorrect factor.
This correction generalizes to any number of repeated groups, each additional group of identical items contributes its own factorial term to divide out of the total.
8. Permutations in AI: Search Space Size

The number of possible orderings for a combinatorial optimization problem, such as the traveling salesman problem visiting n cities, grows as roughly n factorial, an astronomically large search space that motivates the heuristic and approximate search methods covered throughout applied optimization.
This exact factorial explosion is why exhaustively checking every possible ordering becomes impossible past even a modest number of cities or items, motivating approximate algorithms instead.
Even a modestly sized 15-city route planning problem already has over 1.3 trillion possible orderings, making brute force enumeration completely impractical past a small handful of cities.
This is precisely why real routing and scheduling systems rely on heuristic and approximate algorithms rather than checking every possible ordering directly.
9. Permutations in Beam Search

Sequence generation models exploring different possible word orderings, such as in machine translation, are implicitly navigating a permutation space, beam search is a practical technique that keeps only the most promising few partial orderings at each step rather than exploring the full factorial space exhaustively.
Choosing the beam width, how many partial orderings to keep at each step, is itself a tradeoff between exploring more of the permutation space and staying computationally tractable.
A wider beam explores more of the permutation space at the cost of more compute, while a narrower beam is faster but risks missing a better ordering entirely.
10. Circular Permutations

When items are arranged around a circle rather than in a line, rotating the entire arrangement produces what looks like the same circular pattern, so circular permutations of n items are counted as (n minus 1) factorial rather than plain n factorial, correcting for these equivalent rotations.

This same correction appears in problems like arranging people around a circular table or beads on a circular bracelet, wherever rotational symmetry makes certain arrangements indistinguishable from each other.
If the arrangement can additionally be flipped, such as a bracelet that looks the same from either side, an extra division by 2 further corrects for that additional symmetry.
11. Generating Permutations in Code
Python itertools.permutations directly generates every possible ordering of a given collection, useful for small sets where exhaustively checking every arrangement is still computationally feasible.

code.content:
for perm in permutations([1, 2, 3]):
    print(perm)   # prints all 6 orderings one at a time

blocks.text: For larger sets, generating every permutation explicitly quickly becomes impractical, exactly the factorial growth problem covered in section 8, and a sampling or search based approach becomes necessary instead.
Even for a modest 10-item set, there are already over 3.6 million permutations, illustrating why exhaustive generation quickly stops being a viable strategy as the set grows.
12. A Worked Example
A password must use 4 distinct letters chosen and arranged from the 26 letter alphabet. How many distinct passwords are possible?
This password counting example directly applies the without-repetition permutation formula, since the problem explicitly requires 4 distinct letters rather than allowing any letter to repeat.
Increasing the password length or requiring more distinct letters would grow this count very quickly, exactly the same factorial growth pattern covered throughout this lesson.
13. Common Mistakes

items: Using the permutation formula when order does not actually matter, in that case the combinations formula, covered in the next lesson, is the correct one to use instead.
Forgetting to correct for duplicate items when the set to be arranged contains repeated elements, leading to an overcounted result.
Confusing permutations with repetition allowed, n to the power r, with permutations without repetition, the n permute r formula, these give very different results.
Assuming n factorial always gives a reasonably sized number, it grows extremely fast, and can quickly overflow standard integer types or become computationally infeasible for even moderately large n.

blocks.text: A related trap worth naming directly: forgetting that the standard permutation formula assumes no repetition allowed, applying it to a repetition-allowed scenario silently undercounts the true total.
It is also easy to apply the circular permutation correction to a problem that is actually linear, not circular, incorrectly reducing a count that should have used plain n factorial instead.
14. Practice: Count Permutations
A relay race has 6 runners who must be assigned to run in a specific order across 4 legs of the race. How many different orderings are possible?
This relay race scenario is a direct real world instance of the n permute r formula, assigning a specific subset of runners to a specific set of ordered positions.
Try varying the number of legs or runners in this same relay race scenario and observe how quickly the total number of possible orderings grows.
Key Takeaway

A permutation counts ordered arrangements, n factorial for arranging all n items, and n permute r for arranging r items chosen out of n, both formulas built directly from the fundamental counting principle. Order matters, distinguishing permutations clearly from combinations.

The combinations lesson immediately ahead covers the closely related but distinct case where order does not matter, and derives the combination formula directly from the permutation formula covered here.
Circular permutations and duplicate-item corrections, covered in sections 10 and 7, are the two most common special cases layered on top of the basic permutation formula in real counting problems.
Whether counting race finishes, passwords, or search orderings, the same underlying multiplicative logic from the fundamental counting principle drives every formula covered in this lesson.
